option.heading: Method options
reason.rule_f_start: Rule F takes the survey of three years before. The oldest survey with public microdata is 2008, so Rule F's weights start in 2011.
reason.rule_u_end: Rule U takes the same year's survey. The newest survey with public microdata is {survey}, so Rule U stops at {month}.
reason.same_before_2026: The two tutoring options differ only from 2026, when ELSTAT's CPI stops weighting tutoring; before that they are the same series.
reason.hospital: The {first}–{last} household surveys' public files leave out hospital services. Putting them back changes the groups' annual-average rates by at most 0.11 points and the gap by at most 0.07 points.
reason.lockdown: Weights from the 2020 survey, a lockdown year with unusual spending.
reason.first_estimate: A first estimate: the weights will be revised once, when the survey of the year before is out.
reason.fixed_lag: Our choice: before our archive existed, survey release dates can't be used, so Rule F is a fixed lag of three years, today's lag.
reason.less_certain: CPI prices for 2009–2010 come from ELSTAT's original tables, an older version of the prices.
reason.coarser_detail: Before 2015, Eurostat's Greek HICP has item indices only for broader categories, so the items within one share its price movement.
reason.same_year_weights: Same-year weights: not a Laspeyres-type index (its weights aren't from before the prices). Shown to compare with studies made after the fact.
reason.hicp_later: Eurostat publishes the HICP's item indices about a week after ELSTAT's CPI, so these combinations update later in the month.
reason.user_cost: Greece has no price index for imputed rent by user cost or net acquisitions.
reason.timing.N: Newest survey up to the year before; revised once when that survey's microdata arrive.

home.title: Inflation is not the same for every household
home.intro1: When prices rise, they don't rise the same for everyone. A household that spends most of its money on food and rent feels it differently from one that spends more on travel or restaurants.
home.intro2: We measure how much prices rose for different groups of Greek households: poorer and richer, renters and owners, pensioners. We use only public data, and we show every step.
home.cta.start: Start here: what this is about
home.euros.lead: Shopping that cost {amount} in {month} costs today:
home.euros.note: Each group's own basket of spending, updated every year as habits change. Latest data: {month}.
home.peak.title: {year} hit the poorest households hardest
home.peak.text: In {year}, prices for the poorest fifth of households rose by {q1} on average, against {q5} for the richest fifth.
home.peak.detail: "Poorest fifth" means the 20% of people with the lowest income, once household size is taken into account. The gap between the two groups was largest in {peakMonth}: {peak} percentage points.
home.card.start.text: What inflation is, why it differs between households, and how to read our charts.
home.why.text: Each group spends differently. The poorest fifth spends about {q1food} of its budget on food, the richest about {q5food}. When food and energy get dearer, as in 2022, poorer households feel more inflation.

income.title: Who is in each income fifth?
income.lead: What a household takes home after tax decides its group. A bigger household needs more money for the same standard of living, so the limits depend on who lives with you.
income.hh.three: Two adults and one more person aged 14 or over
income.size: This household counts as {size} adult equivalents: the first person aged 14 or over counts 1, every other person aged 14 or over 0.5, every child under 14 0.3.
income.source.ours_soon: Our figures are coming soon. They will come from the household budget survey, the same survey our groups are built from.
income.why: Why our figures and Eurostat's differ
income.why1: Our figures come from the household budget survey, the same survey our groups are built from. Eurostat's come from a different survey (EU-SILC), the official source for incomes.
income.why2: Eurostat takes property tax and the self-employed's insurance contributions off income; the household budget survey doesn't. So, for the same people, ours come out a little higher. Eurostat's figures also describe the year before the survey.

calc.how.title: How it is calculated
calc.how.text: Each category keeps the starting household's own mix inside it: if you raise housing, rent, electricity and heating rise together, in the same proportions, every year. Prices are ELSTAT's official ones. The calculator covers {from} onward.
